claims.claim: **HHS = serum hyperosmolality, hyperglycaemia and dehydration without ketoacidosis** — a medical emergency with **higher morbidity and mortality than DKA**.
claims.source_text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) is a medical emergency of serum hyperosmolality, hyperglycaemia and dehydration without ketoacidosis … HHS also carries a higher morbidity and mortality than DKA
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Biochemical criteria:** glucose over 33.3 mmol/L · venous pH over 7.25 (arterial over 7.30) or bicarbonate over 15 mmol/L · negative or small ketonuria, absent-to-mild ketonaemia · serum osmolality over 320 mOsm/kg.
claims.source_text: Serum glucose >33.3 mmol/L Venous pH >7.25 (or arterial pH >7.30) or bicarbonate >15 mmol/L Negative or small ketonuria, absent to mild ketonaemia Elevated serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.source_text: Serum osmolality = 2 x (sodium) + glucose + urea mmol/L
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Versus DKA:** onset over days to weeks (DKA hours to days); ketones under 3 mmol/L (DKA over 3); dehydration severe and often underestimated. **Kussmaul breathing points to DKA.**
claims.source_text: Distinguishing HHS from DKA HHS DKA Serum glucose … Serum ketones Ketones <3 mmol/L (may be mildly elevated if severely dehydrated) Ketones >3 mmol/L Onset Days to weeks Hours to days Dehydration Severe, often underestimated May be overestimated … deep sighing respiration (Kussmaul breathing) is a sign of DKA
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Risk factors:** obesity, undiagnosed or uncontrolled (especially type 2) diabetes, acute illness or substance use, very high carbohydrate intake, and drugs such as corticosteroids, atypical antipsychotics, phenytoin and beta-blockers.
claims.source_text: Obesity Undiagnosed or uncontrolled diabetes, especially type 2 diabetes Acute illness, stress or substance use Very high carbohydrate consumption Medications eg corticosteroids, atypical antipsychotics, phenytoin, beta-blockers
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Dehydration is usually severe and under-recognised** — hyperosmolality preserves intravascular volume and masks signs. **Assume at least a 12–15% deficit.**
claims.source_text: Caution: dehydration is usually severe and under-recognised. Hyperosmolality maintains intravascular volume and masks clinical signs. Assume at least 12-15% fluid deficit
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Urgent senior, ICU or retrieval consultation for every child with HHS; manage in paediatric HDU or ICU where possible.**
claims.source_text: All children with HHS require urgent consultation with a senior clinician, ICU or relevant retrieval team … Where possible, children and adolescents with HHS should be managed in a paediatric high dependency or intensive care unit
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bloods:** glucose, venous gas, UEC with calcium, magnesium and phosphate, FBC, bedside ketones, blood cultures if febrile; urinary ketones. **Consider an ECG if potassium will be delayed — hypokalaemia is common.**
claims.source_text: Blood glucose Venous blood gas (VBG) Urea, creatinine and electrolytes (UEC) and calcium, magnesium and phosphate (CMP) Full blood count (FBC) Blood ketones (bedside test, normal <0.6 mmol/L) Blood cultures if febrile or suspicion of sepsis Urinary ketones Consider ECG if potassium results will be delayed as hypokalaemia is common
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Shocked: 0.9% sodium chloride 10–20 mL/kg IV bolus**, repeated if needed to restore perfusion, with senior/ICU/retrieval discussion.
claims.source_text: If shocked, administer 10-20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride IV bolus. Repeat if required to restore peripheral perfusion and discuss with senior clinician, intensive care unit (ICU) or retrieval team
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Then full maintenance plus the estimated deficit (typically 12–15%) over 24–48 hours.** Hypotonic maintenance (e.g. 0.45% sodium chloride) is likely needed to reduce osmolality — **only under ICU/retrieval guidance**; use 0.9% if perfusion is poor, the child is unstable, or hypotonic fluid is unavailable.
claims.source_text: Deliver ongoing IV fluid as full maintenance fluids + estimated fluid deficit (typically 12-15%) over 24-48 hours The child will likely require hypotonic maintenance fluid (eg 0.45% sodium chloride) to reduce osmolality. This should only be done under guidance of an ICU/retrieval team If child has ongoing poor perfusion or is haemodynamically unstable, or where hypotonic fluids are unavailable, consider 0.9% sodium chloride maintenance fluid.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Replace urine output, with 0.45% sodium chloride where possible** (urine will be hypotonic).
claims.source_text: Monitor and replace urine output (where possible, replace urine output with 0.45% sodium chloride, as urine will be hypotonic)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Total-body potassium is depleted: keep serum potassium 4–5 mmol/L.** ⚠️ **Do not replace potassium if anuric or above 5.5 mmol/L.** Once insulin starts, check potassium within 1 hour and 2–4-hourly; ECG and cardiac monitoring.
claims.source_text: Children with HHS have a deficit of total body potassium Maintain serum potassium between 4-5 mmol/L Do not replace potassium if patient is anuric or serum potassium is >5.5 mmol/L If insulin is commenced, check serum potassium within one 1 hour and 2-4 hourly thereafter … ECG and cardiac monitoring are required to recognise early signs of potassium derangement
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Corrected sodium = measured sodium + 0.3 × (glucose − 5.5) mmol/L.** Sodium may rise at first; **aim for a fall of 0.5 mmol/L/hour.** ⚠️ Sodium failing to rise as glucose falls, or new hyponatraemia, suggests over-correction and **raises cerebral oedema risk**.
claims.source_text: Corrected sodium = measured sodium + 0.3 x (glucose – 5.5) mmol/L … Aim for a decrease in sodium of 0.5 mmol/L/hour If sodium does not rise as the glucose falls during initial treatment, or if hyponatraemia develops, this may indicate excessive fluid correction and increases risk of cerebral oedema
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Phosphate:** severe hypophosphataemia raises rhabdomyolysis risk — consider potassium-containing phosphate preparations, monitoring potassium hourly. **Magnesium:** replace only in severe cases.
claims.source_text: Severe hypophosphataemia may increase risk of rhabdomyolysis Consider replacing phosphate in preparations that contain potassium, to replace phosphate and potassium simultaneously (monitor potassium levels hourly during replacement) … Consider magnesium replacement in severe cases and monitor serum magnesium levels
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Only give insulin after adequate fluid resuscitation.** Glucose should fall on fluids alone (initially 4–5 mmol/hour); a faster fall in glucose and osmolality can cause circulatory collapse.
claims.source_text: Only administer insulin following adequate fluid resuscitation and rehydration Blood glucose level (BGL) should initially fall with adequate rehydration alone (initially 4-5 mmol/hour, and gradually slowing). A more rapid fall in BGL and osmolality may decrease intravascular volume and lead to circulatory collapse
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start an IV insulin infusion when glucose falls less than 2–3 mmol/L/hour on fluids alone.** The rate is **lower than in DKA.** ⚠️ **No subcutaneous insulin and no insulin bolus.**
claims.source_text: Start IV insulin infusion when BGL decreases at a rate <2-3 mmol/L/hour with fluids alone Insulin infusion is lower in HHS than in DKA, due to relative insulin sufficiency and less ketosis Do not give subcutaneous insulin or insulin bolus
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If glucose fails to fall as expected, reassess renal function.** After recovery, many children with type 2 diabetes need insulin only temporarily.
claims.source_text: Failure of expected fall in glucose should prompt reassessment of renal function … Following recovery many children with type 2 diabetes and HHS will require insulin treatment only temporarily, and many can be managed effectively with diet and oral agents ongoing
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Watch for** venous thrombosis (especially with central lines), rhabdomyolysis, malignant hyperthermia, compartment syndrome, **cerebral oedema from rapid correction**, and ventricular arrhythmias.
claims.source_text: Venous thrombosis, especially with central venous catheters Rhabdomyolysis Malignant hyperthermia Compartment syndrome Cerebral oedema, may result from rapid correction of hyperglycaemia/hyperosmolality Ventricular arrhythmias, secondary to electrolyte disturbance
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Manage in a unit with frequent, timely laboratory access and paediatric HDU/ICU.**
claims.source_text: Children and adolescents with HHS should be managed in a unit that has: Access to laboratory services for frequent and timely evaluation of biochemical variables Paediatric high dependency or intensive care unit
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state' (Last updated July 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hyperosmolar_hyperglycaemic_state/, retrieved 2026-09-23
